svg.text: Traducción
Traduciendo a inglés con Google Translate...
A black hole is a region of space described by Einstein's equations, whose interior contains
a concentration of mass high enough to generate a gravitational field such that, except for
certain types of quantum processes, no particle or radiation—not even light—can escape from
it [1] (in 2021, light reflections were observed in the farthest part of a black hole). [2]
Black holes may be capable of emitting a type of radiation, Hawking radiation, conjectured
by Stephen Hawking in the 1970s. The radiation emitted by black holes, such as Cygnus X-1,
does not originate from the black hole itself but from its accretion disk. [3][4]
The gravity, or "curvature of spacetime," of a black hole creates a singularity enclosed by
a closed surface called the event horizon. This is predicted by Einstein's field equations.
The event horizon separates the region of the black hole from the rest of the universe, and
once inside, no particle, whether material or electromagnetic, can escape, not even photons.
This curvature is studied by general relativity, the theory that predicted the existence of
black holes and provided the first clues to their possible existence. In the 1970s, Stephen
Hawking, George Ellis, and Roger Penrose proved several important theorems about the
occurrence and geometry of black holes. [5] Earlier, in 1963, Roy Kerr had shown that in
four-dimensional spacetime, all black holes must have a quasi-spherical geometry determined
by three parameters: their mass M, their total electric charge e, and their angular momentum
L.
